caption:
A Google patent filing describes "My Channel", a TV channel of AI-made shows where you are the main character.
It would use your watch history and demographic data, and could build your likeness and a synthetic voice from your photos and videos.
An ad server would insert ads into each show. The examiner rejected the application, but Google can still amend or appeal.

Would you watch a show starring yourself?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: 404 Media, Gizmodo · Photo: Google LLC patent filing via Gizmodo

paragraphs.text: A Google patent application describes a system called "My Channel" that would fill a television channel with AI-generated shows built around a single viewer, who would appear as the main character, according to reports from 404 Media, Gizmodo and Cointelegraph published on November 23 and 24, 2026. The filing was first spotted by the patent tracking site Patentlyze, 404 Media reported.

Cointelegraph reported that Google submitted the application on May 13, 2025, and that the US Patent and Trademark Office published it in November 2026. The publication names two Google employees as inventors, Aravind Reddy Ayuluri and Prameela Kavya Thummuru, according to Cointelegraph. 404 Media gave the filing's title as "creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user."

According to Gizmodo, the channel would sit on the TV home screen, and selecting it would bring up a set of show options personalized to the viewer's profile. The filing says shows could be created when a user asks for one or without a specific request, Gizmodo reported. The genres listed in the application include a sci-fi adventure, a romantic comedy, a crime and comedy caper and an action thriller, with a sample viewer named John cast as the protagonist, according to 404 Media.

To personalize the content, the system would draw on the viewer's demographic data, video watch history and other information about the user, 404 Media reported. Gizmodo wrote that a language model would analyze the viewer's most watched videos and shows, and that the genre, themes, pacing, narrative structure and aspect ratio of each generated show would follow that viewing history.

Cointelegraph reported that the system could use photos or videos of the viewer to build a digital likeness and generate a synthetic voice for the character's dialogue. One example in the filing describes a viewer who watched highlights of a cricket player receiving a video that places the viewer at the Cricket World Cup, for instance cheering in the stands, according to 404 Media and Cointelegraph.

The application also covers advertising. According to Gizmodo and 404 Media, a finished show could be passed to an advertising stitcher that inserts at least one advertisement before the content reaches the viewer. Cointelegraph described the flow as an ad server retrieving the generated video, adding ads and streaming the result to the viewer's television.

The application has not been approved. Gizmodo, citing Patentlyze, reported that the patent examiner rejected it, though Google could still amend the application or appeal. None of the reports gave a date for the rejection. Google did not immediately respond to requests for comment from 404 Media or Gizmodo, and Cointelegraph said it had contacted the company.

Patent filings often describe ideas that never become products, and nothing in the reports indicates that Google plans to launch a channel like this. The filing still shows how a large platform with years of viewing data could combine generative video, personal likeness and advertising in a single service, and it puts questions about consent for a person's face and voice, and about how viewing data is used, into concrete terms.
The next signal to watch is whether Google amends or appeals the rejected application, and whether any personalized AI video features appear in YouTube or Google TV products.
